messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The rupture in Arjun’s life began in a cramped kitchen three years ago, when his then-partner, enraged over a missed utility bill, shoved him against the counter. The air grew heavy with the sharp tang of sweat from their escalating argument, and his ex’s voice had dropped into a specific, cutting cadence about responsibility and control before a heavy strike landed against his ribs. Arjun had frozen, certain he should have been able to de-escalate the situation, but his body had locked up as the violence surged. Now, encountering that same olfactory sharpness or hearing a similar conversational turn instantly summons the full memory of that kitchen back to him. These sudden intrusions convince him that his own body keeps reacting as if he is still trapped, cementing a quiet conviction that he could never rely on himself when danger actually arrived. The way the event returns has fundamentally altered how he reads his surroundings. Each time the rage and emotion of the past floods his system, his mind automatically projects that violence onto the present, making him feel genuinely threatened whenever strangers approach him in the store, even for a simple transaction. This heightened sense of imminent danger is compounded by his own self-blame; he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop the abuse, and that inaction guilt seeps into his awareness, making the traumatic memory feel even more vivid and inescapable. Because he views his own reactions as a betrayal, the threat he perceives from ordinary customers begins to feel inescapable, and his fear of strangers approaching in mundane situations becomes a constant, grinding weight. As the weeks turned into months, the cycle tightened around him. He began to believe that his continued guilt and belief in his own frailty actually sharpened his sensitivity to the kitchen’s olfactory cues and conversation topics, making ordinary triggers feel overwhelmingly potent. Simultaneously, his inability to sleep or feel safe at night pushed him to constantly scan his environment, which in turn made him hyper-attuned to those same triggers, forcing him to brace for impact the moment a customer’s voice rose or a familiar smell drifted past the shop window. This relentless scanning made every approaching stranger feel like a direct threat, and that mounting dread soon looped back, causing new memories of the abuse to surface with brutal clarity during the day. When those memories returned, they quickly spiraled into a fresh wave of self-directed blame, convincing him once again that his own body was fundamentally unsafe. The cumulative toll of this exhausting loop eventually fractured his daily life. Arjun found himself avoiding the back entrance of his shop, fearing the sudden closeness of delivery drivers and the smell of their sweat, which now felt like a direct line to the past. He stopped answering calls about finances, knowing those topics would instantly plunge him into the rage and panic of the original confrontation. His partner noticed how distant he had become, how he flinched at casual touches and refused to leave the house after dusk because the night vigilance made the walls feel like they were closing in. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in the shop aisle where a customer’s casual comment about a “slip-up” triggered a full-body freeze, leaving him certain he would never recover his capacity to feel safe again. He hopes to find a way to quiet the noise in his head, though he fears that stepping into therapy will only force him to confront the very memories he has spent years trying to outrun.
